issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, this appraisal is a poor thematic fit because it implies an interpersonal perpetrator threat ('who will harm you') rather than danger from impersonal environmental forces. The rest of the profile is built around disaster-related ongoing danger/hypervigilance and intrusive reliving, so this item stands out as clinically incongruent with the specified trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe classic fear-based re-experiencing and hypervigilance, but there is no accompanying content suggesting perpetration, moral injury, or a specific action during the disaster that would plausibly drive a strong violated-values appraisal.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' could occur after a disaster, but here it sits awkwardly with the otherwise generic fear/reliving profile. There are no memory or threat items about failing to protect family, losing dependents, or role-related guilt, so this item lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'I need to stay alert' while trying to sleep is more characteristic of an ongoing human threat context than of a completed natural disaster, especially when paired with scanning exits and staying near exits in all buildings. Taken together, these threat items imply anticipation of intentional attack or entrapment rather than the specific threat structure suggested by the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is not impossible, but it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile for a 65-year-old married male retail worker with natural-disaster trauma. The rest of the profile centers on ongoing danger, hypervigilance, and intrusive reliving; this item instead implies a specific role-based self-evaluation that is not supported by the other selected appraisals, memory, threat, or coping items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'Other-Blame Rumination' sits awkwardly with a natural-disaster trauma profile. Blame can occur, but this item specifically focuses on dwelling on what other people have done to me, whereas the rest of the profile describes threat and reliving linked to impersonal environmental danger rather than interpersonal harm or betrayal. Without any corroborating appraisal or memory content involving preventable human actions, this item is clinically hard to reconcile.

vignette: John, a 65-year-old African American man, has been struggling with persistent symptoms following his experience of a devastating tornado that hit his hometown last year. Married and working at a local retail store, John's life has dramatically changed since the traumatic event. On the night of the disaster, John was in his home when he heard the roar of the storm approaching. The winds were ferocious, and debris rained down on his house with a relentless intensity. The roof ripped off, and as glass shattered all around him, John could only focus on protecting himself and his family from harm. The memory of that night still haunts him; it plays over in his mind like a film reel, reliving the moment with such vividness that he feels as though he is right back there. John's experience of the tornado has left him deeply convinced that the world is an inherently dangerous place, and that any moment could bring another threat. He constantly scans his surroundings for signs of danger, looking for exits in every room or building he enters. At work, this means he stays near the exit, making sure to keep a clear path to safety. The distraction provided by his job has helped him cope to some extent, but it also makes it difficult for him to fully engage with customers and colleagues. At night, John finds himself struggling to fall asleep because he needs to stay alert. His hypervigilance does not stop once the sun sets; rather, it intensifies as he lies awake in bed, his mind racing through worst-case scenarios. The memory of the tornado feels so present that it is as if the event is happening all over again, which has made him certain that he has permanently changed for the worse. John's hypervigilance extends to his daily routine and interactions at work. He spends a significant amount of time checking and rechecking his surroundings, ensuring there are no signs of potential threats. This constant vigilance has led to several instances where John was distracted during customer service interactions, causing frustration among both customers and his manager. Over the past few months, these episodes have become more frequent, leading to strained relationships at work. In addition to these challenges, John's marriage has been affected as well. His wife often feels neglected because of his need for constant vigilance and distraction from their home life. She notices that he becomes distant when they talk about going out or even having a quiet evening together, which is a stark contrast to the man she once knew. Despite these struggles, what frightens John most is the fear that he will never be able to return to his previous state of mind and that every moment could bring another disaster. He understands that his hypervigilance and constant scanning for exits are maladaptive strategies that have become habitual over time, but they offer him a false sense of security. It was during one particularly difficult night at work, where he felt completely overwhelmed by the memories of the tornado, that John decided to seek help. He realized that these symptoms were taking a toll on his ability to function both personally and professionally. While he is scared about what therapy might reveal or demand from him, he hopes for a future where he can regain some sense of normalcy and no longer feel as though he has permanently changed for the worse. In seeking help, John is most hoping that he can find ways to manage his hypervigilance and the intrusive memories so that he can return to a more balanced life. He wants to be able to engage fully with his work and family without being constantly on guard or feeling like every moment could bring another disaster.
